title: The Convalescent: Prelude-and-Fugue No.13, Book I
content_blocks: I wrote in “The Optimist” (August 1, 2025) about the eager, impatient, overflowing Prelude and Fugue No.12.  Most unusually, the fugue subject jumps the gun, starting before the prelude is even over, and entering early throughout the rest of the fugue.  That same note—B—jumps in again at the end of the piece and holds over into the start of No.13, knitting them together into one big Prelude/Fugue/Prelude/Fugue.

But that impatience leads to a piece that is completely different from all the others in Book I. First, this Prelude and Fugue is the only one in the entire set to use a traditional mode: the Lydian mode, a hopeful version of the well-known major mode (see my Explainer post, tomorrow). That hopefulness may be why the Lydian mode is traditionally associated with convalescing and healing (see, for instance, this movement of Beethoven’s String Quartet Op.132). That association made the Lydian appropriate to this piece: written toward the end of the tumultuous and difficult 2020, it was dedicated “To a Convalescing Nation,” in the hope that we would speedily recover from the malaise that had afflicted us back then.

The prelude explores the use of rich chords moving up and down in parallel to create a sedate, hopeful, and transcendental quality.  As with Prelude-and-Fugue No.7, there are musical spirals:  individual passages of the prelude are the same as upside-down-and-backward versions of themselves, creating a sense of timelessness.  And as with No.7, the prelude continues into the fugue, temporarily producing an accompanied fugue—although once the fugue starts we realize that the fugue melody had already been heard at least three times in the prelude.  Capping off Book I, this is a five-voice fugue (the only other five-voice fugue is the last one in Book II), staying stubbornly within that Lydian mode for the entire duration.  In the end, the consoling harmonies of the prelude return, creating a calm and beautiful conclusion of the set.
David Kaplan creates a rich and consoling performance of this prelude-and-fugue, which you can hear here, or you can watch a video of Numbers 12 and 13 played without a break.
Dedicated in 2020 “To a Convalescing Nation,” in the hope that we would speedily recover from the malaise that had been afflicting us.
